precedents.case_title: Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority
precedents.key_principle: Earnest money or security deposit cannot be forfeited arbitrarily. Section 74 mandates that damages are payable only to the extent of actual proven loss. Unreasonable forfeiture of an entire deposit without proving loss constitutes an unlawful penalty.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Landlord cannot pocket the full security deposit when tenant vacates early if the landlord incurs no actual financial loss or quickly re-rents the property.
precedents.discussion_phrase: As established by the Supreme Court in Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority, (2015) 4 SCC 136, deposit deductions under Section 74 can only compensate for actual proven damages, not punitive forfeiture.

precedents.key_principle: The Indian Contract Act explicitly does not recognize penalty clauses. Even if an agreement states an amount 'shall stand forfeited', courts will only award genuine pre-estimated reasonable compensation.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Nullifies contract clauses claiming 100% forfeiture of security deposit or multiple months rent for premature departure during lock-in periods.
precedents.discussion_phrase: Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, as held by the Constitution Bench in Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass, (1964) 1 SCR 515 / AIR 1963 SC 1405, contract penalty clauses are void to the extent of unreasonable enrichment; compensation is capped strictly at actual justifiable loss.

precedents.case_title: Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (Applied to Lock-in Penalties)
precedents.key_principle: Forfeiture of entire remaining lock-in period rent is an unenforceable penalty under Section 74 unless the landlord proves the premises remained vacant and incurred actual unmitigated loss.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Bars landlords from extracting 6-12 months of unearned rent when a tenant moves out early due to job relocation or emergency.
precedents.discussion_phrase: Under Section 74 and the Constitution Bench ruling in Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass, (1964) 1 SCR 515 / AIR 1963 SC 1405, lock-in penalties cannot exceed the landlord's actual loss during vacancy; rent cannot be collected twice if re-let.

precedents.case_title: Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor
precedents.statute_ref: Transfer of Property Act, 1882 — Section 105 & Indian Easements Act, 1882 — Section 52
precedents.key_principle: Laid down the cardinal test distinguishing a lease from a license. If the document gives exclusive possession of the property against all others, it creates a lease/tenancy, regardless of whether the agreement is titled 'Leave and License'.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Protects tenants from landlords using artificial 'license' titles to bypass statutory tenancy protections when exclusive possession of the flat was handed over.
precedents.discussion_phrase: Under the Supreme Court ruling in Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, (1960) 1 SCR 368, granting exclusive physical possession establishes tenancy protections that cannot be stripped simply by labeling the contract a license.

precedents.case_title: C.M. Beena & Anr. v. P.N. Ramachandra Rao
precedents.key_principle: Courts look past clever drafting to examine the real substance, conduct of parties, and operational reality. A licensee who exercises exclusive control and custody is legally treated with tenancy rights, preventing arbitrary unilateral summary cancellation.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Prevents landlords from asserting arbitrary summary eviction rights by disguising a residential rental agreement.
precedents.discussion_phrase: The Supreme Court in C.M. Beena & Anr. v. P.N. Ramachandra Rao, (2004) 3 SCC 595 established that operational possession and conduct prevail over one-sided contractual terminology; termination rights must be reciprocal.

precedents.case_title: Bishandas & Ors. v. State of Punjab & Ors.
precedents.statute_ref: Constitution of India — Article 21 & Specific Relief Act, 1963 — Section 6
precedents.key_principle: No person in peaceful possession of immovable property can be evicted by force or executive action without due process of law, even after the expiration of a license or lease term.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Landlords are strictly prohibited from changing door locks, disconnecting water/power, or using muscle power to throw out a tenant.
precedents.discussion_phrase: Under the Constitution Bench ruling in Bishandas & Ors. v. State of Punjab, AIR 1961 SC 1570 / (1961) 2 SCR 189, any dispossession without due process of law or court order is illegal, even if the agreement has expired.

precedents.case_title: Ramesh Chand Ardawatiya v. Anil Panjwani
precedents.statute_ref: Specific Relief Act, 1963 — Section 6 & Transfer of Property Act, 1882 — Section 108(c)
precedents.key_principle: A person in settled possession is entitled to protect their possession and quiet enjoyment against the entire world, including the true owner, except through lawful court decree.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Protects tenant against unannounced landlord entry, physical harassment, or arbitrary lockouts.
precedents.discussion_phrase: Settled possession is legally protected under the Supreme Court ruling in Ramesh Chand Ardawatiya v. Anil Panjwani, (2003) 7 SCC 350; landlords cannot disrupt peaceful possession outside judicial process.

precedents.case_title: Anthony v. K.C. Ittoop & Sons & Ors.
precedents.statute_ref: Registration Act, 1908 — Section 17 & Transfer of Property Act, 1882 — Section 106
precedents.key_principle: When an unregistered lease exceeding 11 months is executed, it fails to create a long-term lease due to Section 49 of the Registration Act, but creates a month-to-month tenancy terminable by 15 days notice under Section 106 of TPA.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Explains why standard residential agreements in India are limited to 11 months to avoid compulsory registration and stamp duty expenses while retaining mutual termination flexibility.
precedents.discussion_phrase: As clarified by the Supreme Court in Anthony v. K.C. Ittoop & Sons & Ors., (2000) 6 SCC 394, 11-month leases operate under monthly tenancy norms of Section 106 TPA to maintain mutual flexibility.

precedents.case_title: Statutory Principle: Section 108(m) Reasonable Wear & Tear
precedents.key_principle: A tenant is bound to restore the property in as good a condition as received, subject only to reasonable wear and tear and damage by act of God. Automatic deductions of full painting costs without accounting for natural weathering are legally unsupportable.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Rebuts arbitrary deductions of 1 month's rent for painting when walls only exhibit ordinary aging over 11 months of normal occupancy.
precedents.discussion_phrase: Under Section 108(m) of TPA, tenants are exempt from costs resulting from normal wear and tear; painting charges cannot be arbitrarily deducted without itemized damage invoices.

precedents.case_title: Model Tenancy Act 2021 — Second Schedule Maintenance Division
precedents.court: Parliament of India / Model Tenancy Act
precedents.key_principle: Structural repairs, major civil renovations, external whitewashing, and plumbing line replacements are solely the landlord's responsibility. Tenants are only responsible for routine internal fixtures.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Protects tenants from clauses forcing them to pay for building structural flaws, water seepage, or terrace leakage repairs.
precedents.discussion_phrase: Under Schedule II of the Model Tenancy Act, structural maintenance is the landlord's obligation; tenants cannot be charged for structural defects.

precedents.case_title: Model Tenancy Act 2021 — Section 20 Essential Services Protection
precedents.court: Parliament of India / Model Tenancy Act
precedents.key_principle: No landlord shall, either directly or through any person, cut off or withhold essential services and utilities (water supply, electricity, sanitation, elevator access) enjoyed by the tenant, even in cases of rent dispute or delay.
precedents.tenant_benefit: Strictly bars landlords from cutting off power, water, or internet to pressure tenants during disputes or late rent payments.
precedents.discussion_phrase: Under Section 20 of the Model Tenancy Act, cutting off water or electricity for rent delays is strictly unlawful.
